title: [Rear View] Sara Duterte’s farewell walk?
summary: This is not a declared presidential candidate showing off the breadth of her political coalition. This is more like one thanking the people who stood by her as she prepares her exit.

blocks.text: Is it just me or is Vice President Sara Duterte doing the political version of a farewell walk?

Pageant bekis know the ritual, the one where the reigning queen, before relinquishing her crown, takes a long, almost leisurely walk on the runway, all smiles, waving at the adoring crowd while sentimental music plays in the background.

A pre-recorded speech plays alongside, where she takes stock of her reign, of her experiences and lessons learned, and ends with grateful thank yous to the organization and her fans. The camera follows her as she fades into the background. Behind the curtains, she no longer holds the spotlight, and she knows it.
Watch the Vice President these past days and you will see that walk.

A round of visits to Duterte strongholds, a profuse thanks to supporters for keeping her strong despite adversities, a year-end thanksgiving brunch with political personalities known for loyalty, but no heavyweights who signal leverage and clout.
This is not a declared presidential candidate showing off the breadth of her political coalition. This is more like one thanking the people who stood by her as she prepares her exit.
The whisper in political circles is that the 14 votes needed to convict are there.

Until the votes are in, it remains a whisper, and who knows, the Vice President might pull off a surprise in the Q&A or the Marcos administration’s operators might trip at the runway. But the Duterte camp surely has heard the whisper, and its behavior says it believes the whisper.

The impeachment trial resumes on Tuesday, December 1, and if the schedule holds, the verdict could come before Congress adjourns for Christmas. The verdict will surely be the topic at every family reunion and Noche Buena, along with grumblings over how this administration has made this Christmas season the most miserable since the pandemic lockdown.

Her critics, of course, do not expect her to walk off a winner. The Vice President has long proven she is no Miss Congeniality and after November, certainly not Best in National Costume either. Her defense spent the month showing us how ill-fitting the costume of a public servant living a simple lifestyle is.

The impeachment trial rests on a single article of unexplained wealth. The defense expressed confidence it could make a rebuttal on the prosecution’s forensic report showing alleged unexplained wealth and undeclared assets at P817.87 million. So far, it has failed to make a convincing one.

After announcing, then dropping, 16 bank officials from the list of witnesses, a move that, had it proceeded, would have provided an opening to question her joint account with her father, detained former President Rodrigo Duterte, the defense brought in their anti-money-laundering expert. But the said expert attacked the methodology of a forensic report he admitted he had not read. He also conceded the other claims he made in open court were outside his expertise.

A witness testifying on the banana chip company tied to the Vice President’s husband admitted that the company lacks the property, plant, equipment, and personnel needed to run a manufacturing business. Other witnesses tested the patience of senator-judges with their selective amnesia. Their testimonies only raised more questions and bolstered the case against the Vice President.
And through all of this, the Vice President herself has not taken the stand. The public, says a recent survey, now wants to hear her testify.

In 2012, then-chief justice Renato Corona took the stand at his impeachment trial. He was convicted anyway, but he showed up for his own Q&A. Sara Duterte has chosen to let her lawyers do the talking for her. That’s no way to keep the crown.

When the senator-judges hand in their scorecards, and if the whisper turn out to be true, it would be difficult, if not impossible, for the Vice President to wave and smile, or deliver a generous and sincere thank you for the memories. – Rappler.com
Joey Salgado is a former journalist, and a government and political communications practitioner. He served as spokesperson for former vice president Jejomar Binay.
